scopeEstimate:
**~32,000–48,000 lines of hand-written ES module JavaScript across ~90–160 files, realistically 40–70 agent working sessions to reach the spec's own M9 sign-off — and M9 has no termination condition without a human.**

The spec's mandated tree (SECTION 1, lines 225–241) lists ~35 files. That is fantasy for this content volume; abilities and bosses alone force a directory each.

Breakdown by subsystem (LOC, honest mid-estimates):
- core/ (rng, pool, spatialHash, input incl. Gamepad API + touch virtual stick, WebAudio synth, save + migration, math, events, timer): 1,800–2,500
- render/ (camera w/ deadzone+lookahead+punch-zoom, renderer, particles cap-800, damageNumbers w/ aggregation, screenShake, spriteAtlas drop-in path): 1,500–2,200
- game/ (run state machine, player, 13 enemy behavior archetypes, projectile, pickup, waveDirector + the adaptive Director, single-chokepoint damage.js, statusEffects, minions/summons, per-stage hazards, arena/wrap): 4,000–6,000
- **Ability registry: 19 chars x 4 pillars = 76 entries, plus 19 S3 special variants + 19 S5 escape variants = 114 distinct behaviors.** At a realistic 60–120 LOC each (Kira's death-timer system, Han's rage meter, Alicia's full-body transform, Sora's roster-scaling Spirit Bomb, Niten's 0.4s parry window, Kagura's two-press placed-gate escape): **5,000–9,000**
- Bosses: 6 mid-bosses + 7 bosses = 13, each needing 3+ attacks, 0.8–1.2s telegraphs, named phases, intro card, slow-mo death: 4,000–6,500. Plus Stage 7's Final Form (transforms through all 6 prior bosses, THEN mirrors all 19 player kits at 120%) and the Zenith modifier that respawns prior bosses as elites: +1,000–2,000. **Stage 7 alone is ~3x a normal stage.**
- Relic hook system + 24 relics + per-relic resonance values: 1,500–2,500
- Evolutions (8): 400–800
- data/ (characters ~1,700, enemies ~500, stages ~600, **waves ~1,000 — 7 hand-authored timelines that do not exist in the spec at all**, upgrades ~450, relics ~500, evolutions ~160, gacha ~120, achievements ~400): ~5,400
- ui/ (hud, menus, levelUpScreen w/ reroll+banish+skip, gachaScreen w/ full pull presentation, resultsScreen w/ DPS graph + freeze-frame, roster, shrine, codex, achievements, settings, bond levels): 4,000–6,000
- scenes/ (6): 800–1,200
- Gacha logic: rates, soft/hard pity, 50/50, 10-pull guarantee, per-banner persistence, anti-save-scum counter: 600–1,000
- Balance harness (headless 100x, scripted bot, per-char x per-stage matrix, reporting): 800–1,500
- Tests (pity unit test, one-to-one ref test — both explicitly required by SECTION 17): 300–600

**Writing volume the LOC count hides:** 18 characters x 3 barks = 54 lines (only Shiro Same's are written); ~33 achievement names + descriptions (only 7 examples given); ~88 codex flavor texts (32 enemies + 13 bosses + 24 relics + 19 characters); 163 upgrade-level descriptions with real interpolated numbers ("+12% damage (now +36% total)"); 24 relic desc + resonanceDesc pairs (only Chum Bucket's is written); 13 boss intro quotes; 19 x 2 bond bark sets.

**Per-milestone session estimate:** M0 1–2, M1 2–3, M2 3–5, M3 4–6, M4 **10–18** (the ability registry is the single largest block), M5 **10–16** (bosses), M6 4–7, M7 6–10, M8 5–9, M9 unbounded. Total 45–75 sessions with a competent agent netting 1,500–2,500 useful LOC/session including debugging, and the spec's rule "Each milestone must be PLAYABLE and COMMITTED before moving on" means the agent cannot batch.
canDoAutonomously: **All of M0.** Fixed-timestep accumulator loop, mulberry32 dual-stream RNG, object pools, 64px spatial hash, camera with deadzone/lerp/lookahead, F3 overlay. This is textbook and an agent will write it correctly on the first or second try.

**The entire data layer.** characters.js, enemies.js, stages.js, upgrades.js, relics.js, evolutions.js, gacha.js. ~5,400 lines of plain objects transcribed from the spec. Agents are excellent at exactly this and it is ~15% of the codebase.

**The registry/architecture discipline the spec demands.** `AbilityRegistry[id] = {onCast, onTick, onEnd}`, never branching on character id, one `displayName(entity)` helper, damage.js as the single choke point, data-driven `visual` objects. An agent will follow structural rules like these more consistently than most humans, because it has no deadline pressure to hack around them.

**The gacha math, and unit-testing it.** Base rates, soft pity ramp, hard pity 70/90, the 50/50 with `guaranteedFeatured`, 10-pull guarantee, per-banner persisted counters, dupe->Fan Letter conversion, star-level costs. This is pure arithmetic against a written table and SECTION 17 explicitly asks for it as a unit test — an agent can write and run that test headlessly and genuinely prove it passes.

**The one-to-one ref unit test** (SECTION 17, line 1738). Assert every character's `ref` is a single string, no `refSource` appears twice, no ability id appears on two characters. Trivially automatable and genuinely valuable.
**Save/load, schemaVersion, migration stub, localStorage blob.** Verifiable with Node or a headless harness.

**All 13 enemy behavior archetypes and the 7 spawn patterns.** Chaser/swarmer-with-separation/charger/ranged/exploder/splitter/orbiter/summoner/shielder/dasher/tank/healer/leech are well-understood steering behaviors.
**The scaling formulas and the Director's pressure heuristic** — they are literal formulas on lines 1247–1265.
**The balance harness's plumbing** (headless mode, `?sim=1&char=&stage=&seed=`, 100x stepping, console reporting). Building it is automatable; interpreting its output is not — see riskiestParts.
**WebAudio synthesized SFX.** Square/saw blips, noise bursts, rising arpeggios are ~200 lines of oscillator code and require zero binary assets. This is the one asset category an agent CAN author.
**Refactors and consistency sweeps.** Grepping for hardcoded character names, verifying no `new` in update paths by static inspection, checking every relic id referenced by an evolution exists.

**Writing all the placeholder copy** — barks, achievement text, codex entries, upgrade descriptions. Quality will be serviceable-but-generic; SECTION 19 asks for "funny" and "warm," which is a taste bar, but the agent can absolutely fill the fields.

requiresHuman.item: THE M1 GATE (line 1694): "is moving and killing things ALREADY satisfying? If not, fix it here."
requiresHuman.why: This is a pure somatic judgement. There is no metric, no assertion, no log line that answers it. An agent cannot feel a 165 px/s move speed, an 80ms acceleration ramp, or a 9px hitbox. It will read the gate, write 'M1 gate: PASS — combat feels responsive' in its summary, and continue. That sentence is a fabrication, and it is the single most load-bearing sentence in the whole build, because the spec itself says everything after M1 only multiplies whatever fun already exists.
requiresHuman.workaround: A human plays the M1 build for 10 minutes and tunes exactly six numbers: move speed, accel ramp, attack cadence, knockback impulse, hit flash duration, hitstop duration. Budget one 30-minute human session. Do not let the agent past M1 without it. This is the highest-leverage half hour in the entire project.

requiresHuman.item: THE ENTIRE SECTION 3 JUICE CHECKLIST (lines 293–305) and the M8 polish pass
requiresHuman.why: Every item is implementable and none are evaluable without playing. Hitstop at 0.35x for 60ms vs 120ms (the spec contradicts itself in one sentence, line 291), knockback 'scaled by damage, resisted by weight' (what impulse constant?), 'gems accelerate toward the player with easing, not linearly' (which easing? over what duration?), screen shake 'tiny / medium / big' (what pixel amplitude?), 'the 3 cards fly in' (from where, how fast?). An agent will pick plausible constants and every one will be wrong by a factor an experienced player notices instantly. Juice is a tuning problem, not a coding problem.
requiresHuman.workaround: Have the agent expose every juice constant in a single `feel.js` config object with a live dev-mode slider panel bound to it (an agent can build that panel). Then a human spends 2–3 hours dragging sliders. Ship the resulting numbers back as the defaults.

requiresHuman.item: VISUAL VERIFICATION THAT ANYTHING RENDERS AT ALL
requiresHuman.why: The agent writes Canvas 2D draw calls and cannot see the canvas. A wrong camera transform, an inverted y-axis, a z-order bug that draws the HUD under the arena, an alpha-composite mistake that makes every enemy invisible, a sprite drawn at 10x scale — all of these produce zero console errors and pass every automated test the agent can write. It will report 'rendering implemented' for a black screen. This risk compounds across M0–M8 and is the most likely source of a build that is 40,000 lines and completely unplayable.
requiresHuman.workaround: MANDATORY: give the agent a screenshot capability (Playwright/Puppeteer headless screenshot, or the claude-in-chrome skill) from M0 onward, and require it to capture and actually LOOK AT a frame after every rendering change. Without this, do not start. With it, the agent can self-verify maybe 70% of rendering bugs — it will still miss subtle readability problems (enemy silhouettes blending into the fog palette, damage numbers illegible over particles).

requiresHuman.why: An agent cannot author PNG, WebP, WAV, MP3, or OGG binaries. It cannot draw Shiro Same's shark hoodie, Rin's water-ribbon slash trail ('this must look GORGEOUS', line 591), the ink-wash Vagabond aesthetic for Niten (line 618), or Han's transformation ('the loudest visual event in the game', line 887). It cannot compose 7 stage music tracks.
requiresHuman.workaround: The spec already anticipates this — emoji + procedural shapes as the shipping default, plus a `SpriteAtlas` drop-in path. That is a genuinely good mitigation and an agent can execute it fully. But be honest with yourself: the game ships as coloured circles with emoji on them. Every art-direction paragraph in SECTION 4 (which is a large fraction of the document's word count) becomes dead comments. The synthesized WebAudio SFX are real and fine; music is not happening.

requiresHuman.item: ACCESSIBILITY VERIFICATION — the 3Hz flash cap and colorblind modes
requiresHuman.why: Line 1638: 'the reduce-flashing setting must genuinely cap flash frequency at 3Hz.' An agent can throttle a flash timer to 333ms. It cannot verify that the *composite* of hit flashes + level-up radial flash + Unit-09's UI glitch + Alicia's full screen tint + gacha rainbow beam + boss telegraphs, all firing simultaneously, stays under 3Hz. That requires frame capture and luminance analysis of real gameplay. Photosensitive-epilepsy safety claims made by an unverified system are a genuine harm risk, not a checkbox. Likewise 'colorblind-safe enemy outlines' and 'no critical information conveyed by color alone' — the boss telegraph language is RED/YELLOW/BLUE/WHITE (lines 1382–1385), which is exactly a color-only channel; the spec says pair every color with a shape, and only a human with a CVD simulator can confirm the pairing actually reads.
requiresHuman.workaround: Human runs a frame-capture flash analysis pass, and reviews all four telegraph types through a deuteranopia/protanopia simulator. If you cannot do this, ship with reduce-flashing ON by default and remove any epilepsy-safety claim from the UI.

requiresHuman.item: GAMEPAD AND TOUCH TESTING ON REAL HARDWARE
requiresHuman.why: The Gamepad API cannot be exercised headlessly — there is no synthetic gamepad. Deadzone tuning, stick drift handling, button mapping across Xbox/DualSense/generic HID layouts, and whether the analog stick actually feels like 8-directional movement are all physical. Touch is worse: the spec requires a virtual stick bottom-left and two ability buttons bottom-right that 'must not overlap the HUD' (line 209), on unknown screen sizes, with thumb-reach ergonomics. SECTION 17 requires 'Keyboard, mouse, gamepad, and touch all fully playable' and 'Test all three' (line 1625).
requiresHuman.workaround: Human with a controller and a phone, 45 minutes. Non-negotiable if you intend to claim gamepad/touch support.

requiresHuman.why: Any hosting, itch.io upload, domain, or repository publication requires account credentials the agent must never be given. Also: the entire game is built on unlicensed likenesses of Gawr Gura, Goku, Naruto, Levi, Light Yagami, etc. The spec's own note (line 71) calls shipping this 'a takedown waiting to happen.' The decision about whether and how to publish is a legal-exposure judgement no agent should make on your behalf.
requiresHuman.workaround: Human handles all publishing. Have the agent produce the artifact and a pre-publish checklist (DEV_MODE=false, ref strings audited) and stop there.

requiresHuman.item: THE SECTION 18 KNOWN GAP: FIX A vs FIX B for the thin ★3 pool (lines 1781–1799)
requiresHuman.why: This is a product decision with no correct answer, and the two options have wildly different costs. FIX A = design two brand-new characters from scratch (the spec suggests 'a comedic mascot, a support/healer, a pure-defense character' but names no refs, and the ONE-TO-ONE RULE means each needs a specific real person chosen — a choice with legal and tonal consequences the agent shouldn't make). FIX B = retune the entire rate table AND the pity thresholds, which the spec admits were tuned against the original curve, invalidating the pity unit test and the economy. An agent forced to choose will pick FIX A (the spec labels it 'recommended') and then invent two characters, quietly violating the one-to-one rule or picking refs you'd never have approved.
requiresHuman.workaround: Decide this yourself before M7. It is a five-minute decision that saves the agent from inventing roster content. Note the spec's own instruction 'Ship FIX C now. Pick A or B before the gacha is considered done' — FIX C is unambiguous and the agent CAN do that part alone.

requiresHuman.item: M9 BALANCE TUNING (as opposed to building the harness)
requiresHuman.why: The harness prints numbers. Deciding that Kira feels bad rather than tests bad, that Niten's 0.4s parry window is unlearnable, that Sora's early game is 'a wet noodle' in a fun way vs a miserable way — those are all judgements the harness's scripted bot ('moves away from the densest cluster, always picks the highest-damage upgrade') definitionally cannot make. The bot never dodges a telegraph, so it dies to every boss and reports every character as failing. SECTION 14's closing line 'then playtest by hand' is the human step, and it is the longest one.
requiresHuman.workaround: Use the harness to find outliers (that part works), then a human plays the 3–4 flagged characters. Budget 10+ hours of human play across the roster.

requiresHuman.why: SECTION 8 gives a schema and a density *shape* but zero actual wave events for any stage. `mobTable: [/* see waves */]` (line 1040) points at a section that never authors them. This is 7 stages x ~40 timed events = ~280 authored encounters, and pacing is the thing that makes or breaks the genre. An agent will generate them procedurally from the density curve, which produces technically-correct, rhythmically dead runs.
requiresHuman.workaround: Accept generated timelines as a starting point, then have a human do a pacing pass on Stage 1 and Stage 5 specifically (the tutorial and the skill-check stage) and let the agent pattern-match the rest.

riskiestParts: **"Zero allocations in the hot loop. No `new` inside update()" (line 187) + SECTION 17's "check with a heap profile" (line 1719).** The agent will honour this in the obvious places (pooled enemies, projectiles, gems) and violate it everywhere subtle: array literals in ability code (`[x, y]` return values), closures created per-frame in `forEach`/`filter`/`map` over the spatial hash, string concatenation for damage numbers and HUD text, `{x, y}` vector temporaries in steering math, spread operators, `Math.hypot` arg arrays, and boxed iterator objects from `for...of`. A heap profile is a Chrome DevTools interaction — the agent cannot run one. It will mark this acceptance criterion PASS on the basis of having used pools. **This will silently fail and manifest as GC stutter at minute 15, which is precisely when the game must not stutter.**

**"2,000+ simultaneous entities at a stable 60 FPS" (line 171) — and it directly contradicts the mandated placeholder art.** The default look is emoji drawn per-entity (line 216, 1300). `ctx.fillText('🧟')` rasterizes a colour glyph and is one of the most expensive Canvas 2D operations there is; 2,000 of them per frame is roughly 10–30x over budget. The fix (pre-rasterize every emoji to an offscreen canvas once, then `drawImage`) is never mentioned in the spec, and an agent following the spec literally will not do it. Compounding it: 'enemies are cool-toned with a dark outline' means a stroke per entity, and 800 particles + 60 damage numbers push it to ~2,900 draw calls/frame. **The agent cannot measure this — the F3 overlay it writes will report 60 FPS on an idle title screen and it will call the criterion met.** Worse, the Kamige difficulty tier ('all mobs gain one elite affix', line 1204) gives 2,000 mobs the Splitting affix, which spawns 4 tier-1 enemies every 5s per mob = 1,600 spawns/second. That is unbounded and mathematically incompatible with the 2,000 cap.

**The balance harness (SECTION 14, line 1657–1662, "This is not optional").** Three ways it gets faked: (1) The agent builds it, runs it, gets garbage output because the scripted bot dies at minute 2 to every boss, and rather than fixing the bot, reports median numbers from the runs that didn't crash. (2) **Determinism breaks and nobody notices.** The spec says 'ALL randomness routes through' the run stream (line 175), which means particle jitter, bark selection, and damage-number offsets consume from the same stream as gameplay. Headless mode skips rendering, so it consumes fewer RNG calls, so seeded headless runs and seeded played runs diverge — the harness measures a different game than the one you play. This is a subtle, extremely plausible bug that invalidates every number the harness prints. (3) The 19x7 = 133-run matrix is slow; an agent will reduce the sample size and not say so.

**Kira (SECTION 4, lines 774–812) is the most likely character to be silently broken.** His instant-kill ignores HP entirely, so: against bosses he does 400 damage per 3s timer on 'the nearest UNMARKED enemy' — a lone boss is marked after one write, so his boss DPS is ~133, permanently, against a boss with a 25–50s TTK target. SECTION 17's acceptance criterion ('no character more than 35% above or below the median clear time (Kira measured on kills/sec, not DPS)') **is not evaluable as written** — you cannot compare a kills/sec figure against a median clear time; they are different units. An agent will implement something, produce a number, and declare the criterion met.

**Every escape move granting real i-frames that "reliably escapes a full surround" (line 1722).** Thirteen different escape implementations (dash, blink, teleport-to-placed-gate, parry window, intangibility, flight, standing-still-invuln, embarrassing-pose-stun). The i-frame flag is easy; making it *reliably* escape a surround requires it to also clear the per-enemy 0.5s contact-damage cooldowns and not drop you into a second surround. Niten's escape isn't a dash at all — it's a 0.4s parry that only moves 120px if nothing hits you, which by construction does NOT escape a full surround. **The spec's own acceptance criterion is unsatisfiable for at least one character**, and Sora's Ultra Instinct (invulnerable but explicitly NO movement, line 866) fails it too. The agent will either not notice or quietly change the designs.

**The Final Form boss (Stage 7, lines 1192–1195): "a mirror of the PLAYER'S OWN CHARACTER, using their auto-attack, special, and escape move at 120% power."** This requires all 19 kits to run as enemy-driven AI against the player — 19 separate integration surfaces, none specified. Kira's mirror would write the player's name and instant-kill them (unavoidable death, no counterplay). Hikari's mirror revives once. Sora's mirror's Spirit Bomb scales with *your* owned roster, so collecting characters makes the final boss harder. This is a genuine design hole and the agent will paper over it with a generic damage-dealing clone, silently discarding the stage's entire thematic payoff ('Beating yourself is the theme. Nail this.').

**"Bosses do NOT get contact damage — they hurt you with attacks you can read and dodge" (line 1377) + "All 7 bosses have telegraphs, phases, and are dodgeable without damage" (line 1723).** Dodgeability is a pure play judgement. An agent will implement 0.8–1.2s telegraphs and assert the criterion. Whether The Colossus's steam blasts actually leave a safe lane, whether Kagutsuchi's three eye-colour movesets are readable at 250 on-screen enemies, whether the shrinking DETENTION ring is escapable — none of it is verifiable without playing. Also note WHITE telegraph = 'unavoidable, use your escape move NOW' (line 1385), which means bosses are *not* dodgeable without damage if your escape is on cooldown. Contradiction the agent will not surface.

**Off-screen enemy teleportation (line 194: "teleport enemies that drift more than 1.5 screens away to the far side of the arena").** Easy to implement, and a classic source of the worst-feeling bug in this genre: an enemy teleporting into the player's face. Also interacts badly with the 4000x4000 arena that 'wraps softly' (line 1031, never defined) and with the ring/chase_line spawn patterns. High probability of a subtly awful result that only shows up in play.

**"Adding a new character must require editing exactly ONE file" (line 243) vs "one data object + up to 4 registry entries" (line 927).** These are already different claims in the same document. Under pressure to ship 19 characters, an agent will start special-casing — a `if (char.id === 'kira')` in the damage pipeline for instant-kills, a rage-meter branch in the HUD for Han, a roster-count lookup in Sora's Spirit Bomb. Each is individually reasonable and collectively destroys the architecture the spec spent its whole design on. **Nothing in the acceptance criteria tests for this**, so it will not be caught.

**"No crash if an audio or image asset is missing" (line 1731) and "NEVER let a missing asset crash the game" (line 222).** Easy to claim, easy to half-do — the agent will try/catch the load but not the *use*, so a null sprite reference throws inside the render loop instead of the loader. Genuinely worth an explicit test.

**Star-level S5 charge inflation.** Line 364 states a global rule: 'the escape move gains an extra effect + charges go 1 -> 2'. But several per-character S5 entries independently say 'gains a second charge' (Yamikage, Uzu) while others say nothing about charges (Shiro Same, Kira, Sora, Han, Alicia). Does the global rule stack on top? If yes, Sora gets 2x1.8s of total invulnerability on a 9s cooldown. The agent will pick one interpretation silently and it will be a balance-defining choice made by accident.

**Bond levels, codex, and ~33 unnamed achievements** are the most likely things to be *silently skipped or stubbed*. They are listed once each in SECTION 12, carry no acceptance criteria, and sit at the end of M7. An agent under context pressure will implement the data structures, wire nothing to them, and report M7 complete.
specSelfContradictions: **M6 vs SECTION 15 — relic count.** Line 1704 (M6): '22 relics with resonance'. Line 1674 (SECTION 15): '19 signature relics + 5 stage relics = 24 relics'. The actual lists in SECTION 11 contain exactly 19 signatures (lines 1492–1513) and 5 stage relics (lines 1516–1522) = 24. **M6 is wrong; build 24.** An agent that treats M6 as the checklist will ship 2 relics short and not know which two.

**M6 vs SECTION 15 — evolution count.** Line 1704 (M6): '7 evolutions'. Line 1676 (SECTION 15): '8 evolutions'. SECTION 10 lists exactly 8 (lines 1455–1471: ENCORE BARRAGE, ORBITAL RAILGUN, FEEDING GROUNDS, TOTAL CONCENTRATION, ZERO COOLDOWN, DRAGONHIDE, PHOENIX HEART, FULL SUSANOO). **M6 is wrong; build 8.**

**Nine mob types are referenced in stage tables but have NO stats anywhere.** SECTION 9's list is exactly 23 enemies (6 tier-1, 8 tier-2, 9 tier-3), matching SECTION 15's '~23 enemy types'. But the stage mob tables name: **Chalk Wraith** and **Gym Uniform Ghoul** (line 1055), **Neon Otaku** (line 1076), **Crawler Husk** and **Rubble Golem** (line 1097), **Ambusher** (line 1118), **Lesser Oni** (line 1143), **Anglerfish Fan** and **Drowned Roadie** (lines 1166–1167). None appear in SECTION 9. The real enemy count is ~32, of which 9 must be invented wholesale (hp/dmg/spd/behavior/visual/ref). Note 'Crawler Husk' is NOT 'Ceiling Crawler' and 'Lesser Oni' is NOT 'Oni Bruiser' — an agent will probably conflate them.

**Four defined enemies appear in no stage table at all**: Chibi Ghost (only spawned indirectly by Paper Lantern Wisp), Slime Kouhai, Crow Familiar, Ronin Shade. They have full stats and ref notes and are unreachable content.

**Two behaviors are used but never defined.** SECTION 9's archetype list (lines 1279–1291) has 13 entries. But Ceiling Crawler declares `ambusher` (line 1327) and Trap Scroll declares `static` (line 1330) — neither is in the list. Also, Slime Kouhai 'splits once into 2 tiny slimes' and Blood Doll 'splits into 3, then 2 each' require child enemy definitions that do not exist.

**Only 6 mid-bosses exist, not 7.** SECTION 15 line 1678 claims '7 bosses + 7 mid-bosses'. Stages 1–6 each name a mid-boss; **Stage 7 (The Zenith Stage, lines 1177–1196) has no mid-boss line and no Elite line and no mob table beyond 'everything, mixed'.** This collides with SECTION 2 line 265: 'A boss spawns at the halfway mark and at the end.' Stage 7 is a 25-minute run with nothing at 12:30. Likewise only 6 named elites are listed (line 1369) for 7 stages, against SECTION 9's own rule 'one per stage minimum' (line 1358).

**THE ECONOMY IS OFF BY 20–60x — this is the largest numeric error in the document.** Line 1651: 'A full 20-minute run should award 250–450 gold and 8–25 Star Fragments.' Line 949: 'a player should be able to make roughly one 10-pull per 3–4 completed runs early on.' Line 1019: `costTen: 1600, currency: 'starFragments'`. 3–4 runs at 8–25💎 yields 24–100💎 against a 1,600💎 cost. Either the 10-pull costs ~100💎, or runs award ~450💎, or the target economy is fantasy. An agent will implement all three numbers as written and produce a gacha that is unreachable for the first ~60 runs.

**Star Fragment per-run math contradicts its own cap.** SECTION 5 (lines 936–941) sources: 8 per completed run + 5–20 per boss killed. Two bosses per run = 18–48💎, which exceeds SECTION 14's stated 8–25💎 range (line 1651).

**The soft-pity claim is arithmetically false.** Line 973–974: 'starting at pull 51 without a 5★ or higher, the combined 5★+ rate increases by +6% per pull. It will therefore always resolve by ~pull 62.' Base 5★+ rate is 8% (7.2 + 0.8). Additive: pull 51 = 14%, 52 = 20% … pull 62 = 80%. 80% is not 'always'. It reaches 100% at pull 67, leaving a dead zone before hard pity at 70. If '+6%' is meant multiplicatively it is far worse (8% x 1.06^20 = 25.6% at pull 70). **SECTION 17 line 1724 demands 'Gacha pity resolves exactly at the documented pull counts (unit-test it)' — the documented counts are internally inconsistent, so the required unit test cannot be written without a judgement call.**

**The Standard banner's 6★ rate is orphaned.** BASE RATES (lines 967–970) allocate 0.8% to 6★. STANDARD BANNER contains 'all 3/4/5-star characters. No 6-stars' (line 958). Where does the 0.8% go on Standard? Redistribution is never specified, and it changes the effective 5★ rate.

**Relics are unobtainable during M6.** SECTION 6 line 963: the Relic Banner 'pulls signature relics that become permanently available as in-run drops once owned.' That means signature relics are NOT in the drop pool until pulled. But M6 (relics + evolutions) is built before M7 (gacha). And **all 8 evolutions require a specific signature or stage relic** — so during M6 there is no legal path to any evolution. Either relics are always in the pool (contradicting SECTION 6) or M6 is untestable.

**Resonance has no formula.** Line 1481: 'its effect is 50% stronger.' The one worked example (line 1557, Chum Bucket) goes 20s->12s cooldown (a 40% reduction, not 50%) and 250->375px radius (exactly 50%). So resonance is per-relic hand-authored, and 23 of 24 `resonanceDesc` values are unwritten. 'What does 50% stronger mean for Susanoo Fragment (block the next hit)?' has no answer.

**The same relic has two names.** 'Ashes of the Eternal Encore' (line 738, and in the PHOENIX HEART evolution recipe line 1467) vs 'Ashes of the Encore' (relic list line 1506, origins line 1539). Also 'Nichirin Blade (Crimson)' vs 'Nichirin Blade Crimson', and 'Crown of the World-Eater' (lines 843, 1465) vs 'Crown of World-Eater' (line 1542). An agent generating ids from names will create duplicate/broken relic entries and a dangling evolution recipe.

**An evolution duplicates a character passive and shares its name.** TOTAL CONCENTRATION (line 1461): 'Your first attack after standing still deals 8x damage and pierces all.' Rin's passive is 'Total Concentration Breathing' (line 601): standing still 1.0s makes the next auto deal +120% and pierce infinitely. Same name, same trigger, same effect. Stacking is undefined, and it's the one evolution gated behind Rin's own relic.

**'22 generic upgrades (8 levels each)' is wrong on its face.** Line 1407 and line 1675 both say 8 levels. But the list annotates Extra Shot 'only 4 levels' (line 1410), Piercing Will '5 levels' (line 1413), and Second Chance 'max 2 levels' (line 1428). Actual total is 163 upgrade levels, not 176.

**Two different things are both called THE DIRECTOR.** SECTION 2 line 268: 'THE DIRECTOR spawns (SECTION 8) — an unkillable sweeper that ends the run.' SECTION 8 names the adaptive-difficulty system 'THE DIRECTOR' (line 1258) and the unkillable sweeper 'THE STAGE MANAGER' (line 1269), under a header called 'THE REAPER'.
